Background and Context

Overview Peter Weir’s Picnic at Hanging Rock (1975) opens with a title card dating its events to St Valentine’s Day, 1900: a party of schoolgirls from Appleyard College picnics at Hanging Rock, near Mount Macedon in Victoria, and several members of the party disappear without trace. The film never explains what happened. Instead, it studies how a rigid, ordered colonial society reacts when something happens that its rules, clocks and explanations cannot contain. Knowing where the story comes from, when it is set and how it was made will help you write about Weir’s choices rather than just the plot.

Joan Lindsay’s Novel The film is adapted from Joan Lindsay’s 1967 novel of the same name. Lindsay deliberately blurred fact and fiction, presenting the disappearance as if it might have happened and declining to say whether it did. That ambiguity became part of the story’s legend: many readers and viewers came to believe the events were real. A final chapter that Lindsay cut from the novel, offering a strange, quasi-supernatural resolution, was published after her death; it plays no part in the film.

Analysis You are studying the film, not the novel. Weir keeps Lindsay’s refusal to resolve the mystery and makes it the centre of the viewing experience: the audience, like the characters, is left wanting an answer that never arrives. When you write about ‘unresolved mysteries’, remember that this is a deliberate construction, not a gap.

t: Peter Weir and the Australian New Wave
b: Peter Weir and the Australian New Wave Picnic at Hanging Rock was one of the defining films of the Australian New Wave, a revival of local filmmaking in the 1970s supported by new government film funding. Directed by Peter Weir from a screenplay by Cliff Green, it was a major critical and commercial success and helped bring Australian cinema to international audiences. Appleyard College was filmed at Martindale Hall in South Australia, while the picnic and search scenes were shot at Hanging Rock itself.

t: Peter Weir and the Australian New Wave - Analysis
b: Analysis The New Wave was partly about Australians telling stories about their own landscape and history. Weir’s film looks back at colonial society with a mixture of beauty and unease: the European culture of the college looks lovely but out of place against the ancient Australian bush. This tension between imported civilisation and the land is at the heart of most essay topics.

Victoria in 1900 In 1900 Victoria was still a British colony; Federation would come on 1 January 1901. Wealthy colonial society modelled itself on Britain: its schools taught deportment, French, poetry and the accomplishments expected of young ladies, and its social life was governed by strict rules about class, dress and behaviour. Girls were laced into corsets, gloved and hatted outdoors, and expected to be decorative, obedient and chaste. Class divisions were sharp. The Fitzhuberts are landed gentry; Albert, their groom, is a working man who grew up in an orphanage; Sarah, his sister, is a ward whose fees go unpaid. Mrs Appleyard’s college depends on wealthy parents’ money and on its reputation for respectability.

Analysis The rules of this society explain much of what we see: the gloves Mrs Appleyard allows the girls to remove only ‘once the drag has passed through Woodend’, the horror at Miss McCraw being seen without her skirt, the police assumption that the explanation must be a man. Weir shows how fragile these conventions are once they meet something beyond them.

Hanging Rock Hanging Rock is a volcanic formation in the Macedon Ranges, north-west of Melbourne, and lies on the traditional lands of the Dja Dja Wurrung, Taungurung and Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung peoples. Geologically it is relatively young, a point Miss McCraw makes in the film, but in human terms it is ancient. Its jagged pinnacles, narrow passages and balanced boulders give it the maze-like quality Weir’s camera exploits.

Analysis The colonial characters treat the Rock as a picnic spot and a curiosity to be measured. The film suggests that it existed long before them and will outlast them. The settlers’ lack of any real relationship with the land, including the Indigenous history they overlook, is part of what makes it seem so alien and threatening to them.

t: The Look and Sound of the Film
b: The Look and Sound of the Film Cinematographer Russell Boyd gave the film its dreamy, soft-focus look, with diffused light, slow motion and lingering shots of the landscape. The soundtrack mixes Gheorghe Zamfir’s haunting pan flute, original music by Bruce Smeaton, European classical pieces such as the slow movement of Beethoven’s Fifth Piano Concerto, and an unsettling low rumble associated with the Rock.

t: The Look and Sound of the Film - Analysis
b: Analysis These choices create the film’s central tension between beauty and menace. The images are lovely, almost like paintings, but the sound and pacing keep the viewer uneasy. See the Film Techniques section for how to use them in essays.

t: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
b: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
Social Values

t: Social Values - Order, Rules and Respectability
b: Order, Rules and Respectability Appleyard College values discipline, punctuality and propriety above all. Mrs Appleyard’s instructions before the picnic about gloves, ‘tomboy foolishness’, snakes and returning ‘at about 8’ show a world that tries to anticipate and control every risk. The film questions whether these rules create real order or only the appearance of it: when the girls vanish, the rules offer no answer, and the institution begins to collapse.

t: Social Values - Class and Social Hierarchy
b: Class and Social Hierarchy Wealth and status decide who belongs. Sarah, an orphan whose fees are ‘impossibly overdue’, is excluded from the picnic and treated harshly; Mrs Appleyard insists the college is not a ‘charitable institution’. Michael and Albert’s friendship across the class divide stands out as a rare challenge to these values.

Femininity and Restraint The girls are dressed in white, corseted and gloved, praised for beauty and refinement. The film links this ideal of femininity to repression: the girls who climb the Rock shed their shoes, stockings and gloves, and the community’s reaction to the disappearance focuses obsessively on bodies and sexual danger.
Cultural Values

Rationality and Science The characters trust measurement, investigation and explanation. Miss McCraw studies geometry and geology; Sergeant Bumpher interviews witnesses and organises searches; the doctor examines Irma. The film presents a world that does not yield to these methods, suggesting the limits of a purely rational worldview.

t: Cultural Values - European Culture in the Australian Landscape
b: European Culture in the Australian Landscape The college is a piece of England transplanted to the bush: Botticelli prints, Valentine’s poetry, cultivated flowers, high tea and classical music. Weir sets this imported culture against an ancient landscape it does not understand, revealing the colonists’ sense of being outsiders in the land they occupy.

t: Cultural Values - Romanticism and the Sublime
b: Romanticism and the Sublime Some characters, especially Miranda and Michael, are drawn to nature as something beautiful, spiritual and liberating. This Romantic longing for connection with nature coexists with fear: the Rock is both enchanting and terrifying.
Thematic Quote Bank

Nature as a Fundamental Force Miranda (voice-over): ‘What we see and what we seem are but a dream, a dream within a dream.’ Mrs Appleyard: ‘The vicinity is renowned for its venomous snakes and poisonous ants of various species.’ Mrs Appleyard: ‘The Rock is extremely dangerous, and you are therefore forbidden any tomboy foolishness in the matter of exploration.’ ‘Waiting a million years, just for us.’ Edith: ‘Why can’t we just sit on this log and look at the ugly old rock from here?’ Edith: ‘It’s nasty here.’ Edith (remembering the Rock): ‘It was a cloud... it was red.’

t: The Human Need for Rationality and Control
b: The Human Need for Rationality and Control Mr Hussey: ‘Nobody knows what happened... we were all asleep.’ Sergeant Bumpher (to Edith): ‘Was there a man?’ Mrs Bumpher, reporting local gossip: ‘It couldn’t be local. No one around here would do a thing like that.’ ‘People don’t just disappear... not without good reason.’ A townsman outside the police station: ‘We’ve got a right to know.’ The doctor, examining Irma: ‘It’s very strange.’ The head gardener: ‘There’s some questions got answers, some haven’t.’ Mrs Appleyard, on Irma being the only girl found: ‘This makes it worse.’

Time Miranda, of her watch: ‘Don’t wear it anymore. Can’t stand it ticking above my heart.’ Irma, of Miranda’s watch: she would wear it ‘always... even in the bath.’ Mr Hussey: ‘Blowed if me watch hasn’t stopped... stopped at twelve o’clock.’ Miss McCraw: ‘Stopped at twelve. Never stopped before. Must be something magnetic.’ Marion: ‘I should like to take a few measurements at the base of the rock, if we have time.’ Irma: ‘We’ll be back long before tea.’ Miranda: ‘Everything begins and ends at exactly the right time and place.’ Edith: ‘When are we going home?’ Mrs Appleyard, remembering Bournemouth: ‘Nothing changed – ever.’

Class and Civilisation Mrs Appleyard: ‘You may remove your gloves once the drag has passed through Woodend.’ Mrs Appleyard: ‘Mr Hussey! I shall expect you back, Miss McCraw and Mademoiselle, at about 8.’ Mrs Appleyard: ‘There are several sets of tuition fees which are impossibly overdue... Sarah Waybourne, for instance.’ Mrs Appleyard: Appleyard College is not a ‘charitable institution’. Marion, looking down from the Rock: ‘Whatever can those people be doing down there? Like a lot of ants. Surprising the number of human beings are without purpose. Although it is probable they’re performing some function unknown to themselves.’ ‘How foolish can human creatures be.’ Albert: if ‘the cop... the tracker and the bloody dog can’t find them, no one bloody can.’

Beauty, Innocence and Appearance Mademoiselle de Poitiers: ‘Now I know... Miranda is a Botticelli angel.’ Mademoiselle, embracing Irma on her return: she is ‘prettier than ever’. Mrs Appleyard, to the students: they can ‘thank the Lord for Irma’s merciful recovery’. Miss Lumley, of strapping Sarah to the gymnasium wall: it is ‘for her own good’, to cure her ‘terrible stooping’.
Character Quote Bank

Miranda Miranda leads the girls up the Rock and does not return. Beautiful, serene and drawn to the natural world, she is idealised by almost everyone around her. ‘What we see and what we seem are but a dream, a dream within a dream.’ – the film’s opening voice-over. ‘Don’t wear it anymore. Can’t stand it ticking above my heart.’ – rejecting her jewelled watch at the picnic. ‘Everything begins and ends at exactly the right time and place.’ – on top of the Rock, just before she disappears. ‘Someday, Sarah, you shall have to come home with me to the station... meet my sweet, funny family for yourself.’ – to Sarah on the morning of the picnic. ‘You must learn to love someone else, apart from me.’ – to Sarah, as if anticipating her own absence.

Marion Marion is intellectual and detached, taking measurements on the Rock with a protractor. She does not return. ‘I should like to take a few measurements at the base of the rock, if we have time.’ – asking permission to explore. ‘I do wish you’d stop talking for once.’ – to Edith during the climb. ‘Whatever can those people be doing down there? Like a lot of ants. Surprising the number of human beings are without purpose.’ – looking down on the picnickers from the Rock.

Irma Irma is the heiress of the group and the only climbing girl who comes back, with no memory of what happened. She would wear Miranda’s watch ‘always... even in the bath.’ – at the picnic. ‘We’ll be back long before tea.’ – before the climb. ‘If only we could stay out all night and watch the moon rise.’ – on the Rock. ‘Poor Edith, we’ll be back soon.’ – to Edith before the girls disappear.

Edith Edith is plump, complaining and frightened. She keeps her hat, gloves, shoes and stockings on, and runs screaming from the Rock. ‘Why can’t we just sit on this log and look at the ugly old rock from here?’ – during the climb. ‘It’s nasty here.’ – as the others are drawn further in. ‘When are we going home?’ – repeatedly, during the climb. ‘It was a cloud... it was red.’ – remembering, when she returns to the Rock with Sergeant Bumpher.

Mrs Appleyard The headmistress embodies authority, convention and institutional control. As events slip beyond her control, she unravels. ‘You may remove your gloves once the drag has passed through Woodend.’ – instructions before the picnic. ‘The Rock is extremely dangerous, and you are therefore forbidden any tomboy foolishness in the matter of exploration.’ – warning the girls. ‘Mr Hussey! I shall expect you back, Miss McCraw and Mademoiselle, at about 8.’ – as the drag departs. ‘This makes it worse.’ – chiding Miss Lumley for calling Irma’s discovery ‘wonderful news’. ‘There are several sets of tuition fees which are impossibly overdue... Sarah Waybourne, for instance.’ – as the college faces financial pressure. ‘We shall have to make other arrangements.’ – to Sarah, about her unpaid fees. Bournemouth was ‘a delightful place’ where ‘nothing changed – ever.’ – reminiscing with Mademoiselle at dinner. She had come to ‘depend so much on Greta McCraw’ and her ‘masculine mind’: ‘How could she allow herself to be spirited away?’ – at the same dinner.

Sarah Waybourne An orphan and ward of the college, Sarah is forbidden from the picnic and devoted to Miranda. She is later found dead. Miranda had many ‘secrets’: ‘she knew she wouldn’t come back.’ – after the disappearance. At the orphanage she had her head shaved for telling the matron she wanted to be a ‘circus rider’. – confiding in Minnie.

Miss McCraw The mathematics mistress, admired by Mrs Appleyard for her ‘masculine mind’. She climbs the Rock alone and does not return. ‘Stopped at twelve. Never stopped before. Must be something magnetic.’ – when the watches are found stopped. The Rock is ‘quite young, geologically speaking.’ – explaining its volcanic origin at the picnic.

Mademoiselle de Poitiers The French mistress is warm, romantic and admired by the students, but increasingly anxious for answers. ‘Now I know... Miranda is a Botticelli angel.’ – watching Miranda. Irma is ‘prettier than ever.’ – embracing Irma, before questioning her about what she told the police.

Miss Lumley The junior mistress is timid and fearful of Mrs Appleyard. She eventually resigns. Irma’s discovery is ‘wonderful news.’ – rebuked by Mrs Appleyard. Strapping Sarah to the wall is ‘for her own good’, to cure her ‘terrible stooping’. – in the gymnasium.

Michael Fitzhubert A young English aristocrat visiting his uncle and aunt. He watches the girls cross the stream and becomes obsessed with finding them. ‘I wake up every night in a cold sweat. Just wondering if they’re still alive.’ – to Albert. The girls ‘may be out there dying of thirst.’ – insisting on searching the Rock himself.

Albert Crundall The Fitzhuberts’ groom: earthy, practical and loyal. He finds Irma and, without knowing it, is Sarah’s brother. If ‘the cop... the tracker and the bloody dog can’t find them, no one bloody can.’ – trying to talk Michael out of searching. He dreams of his ‘kid sister’ on the night of Sarah’s death. – telling Michael about the dream.

The Investigators and the Town Mr Hussey: ‘Nobody knows what happened... we were all asleep.’ – reporting to Mrs Appleyard and Sergeant Bumpher. Sergeant Bumpher: ‘Was there a man?’ – questioning Edith. Sergeant Bumpher: ‘As the girls were jumping the creek, what were you thinking of?’ – interviewing Michael, who answers by pointing to a swan vase. Mrs Bumpher: ‘It couldn’t be local. No one around here would do a thing like that.’ – repeating the town’s gossip. A townsman: ‘We’ve got a right to know.’ – outside Bumpher’s house after Irma is found. The doctor: ‘It’s very strange.’ – listing Irma’s injuries. The head gardener: ‘There’s some questions got answers, some haven’t.’ – one of the film’s few direct statements of its idea.
Character Relationships

Mrs Appleyard and Sarah Waybourne The film’s most painful relationship is one of power. Mrs Appleyard is upright, ornately dressed and usually framed above other characters or behind her desk; Sarah is small, plain, stooped and often seated or diminished in the frame. Sarah loves poetry and feeling; Mrs Appleyard values rules and fees. As the college comes under pressure, Mrs Appleyard turns her frustration on Sarah, the one person with no family or money to protect her.

t: Mrs Appleyard and Sarah Waybourne - Key Quotes
b: Key Quotes Mrs Appleyard: ‘There are several sets of tuition fees which are impossibly overdue... Sarah Waybourne, for instance.’ Mrs Appleyard: ‘We shall have to make other arrangements.’ Mrs Appleyard: Appleyard College is not a ‘charitable institution’.

t: Mrs Appleyard and Sarah Waybourne - Key Ideas
b: Key Ideas Class and social hierarchy Authority and cruelty Reason versus emotion Victim or agent of her own fate?

Miranda and Sarah Sarah adores Miranda, who is kind to her and seems to offer belonging. Miranda’s gentle advice that Sarah ‘must learn to love someone else’ reads, in hindsight, like a farewell. With Miranda gone, Sarah is completely alone; just before Sarah’s death, Weir focuses on her photograph of Miranda.

Key Quotes Miranda: ‘Someday, Sarah, you shall have to come home with me to the station... meet my sweet, funny family for yourself.’ Miranda: ‘You must learn to love someone else, apart from me.’ Sarah: Miranda had many ‘secrets... she knew she wouldn’t come back.’
Key Ideas Love and isolation Foreshadowing The cost of the disappearance for those left behind

Michael and Albert Michael is a privileged young Englishman; Albert is the Fitzhuberts’ groom, raised in an orphanage. At the picnic Albert makes crude remarks about the girls while Michael watches them in silence. The search draws them together: Albert rescues Michael from the Rock, and their conversations grow into a genuine friendship that ignores the social hierarchy around them. In their final scene Albert tells Michael about his dream of his ‘kid sister’, a connection to Sarah that neither fully understands.

Key Quotes Albert: If ‘the cop... the tracker and the bloody dog can’t find them, no one bloody can.’ Michael: The girls ‘may be out there dying of thirst.’ Michael: ‘I wake up every night in a cold sweat. Just wondering if they’re still alive.’
Key Ideas Friendship across class Acceptance (Albert) versus the search for understanding (Michael) Instinct and intuition

Albert and Sarah Albert and Sarah are brother and sister, separated in the orphanage. The film never brings them together: Albert does not know his sister is at the college a few miles away, and Sarah does not keep in touch with him. On the night of Sarah’s death, Albert dreams that she visits him to say goodbye.
Key Ideas Class and lost opportunity Mystery and the supernatural Dramatic irony

Mrs Appleyard and Miss McCraw Mrs Appleyard relies on Miss McCraw as the embodiment of reason and order. That the most rational person in the film is ‘spirited away’ shakes Mrs Appleyard’s belief that the world can be controlled.

t: Mrs Appleyard and Miss McCraw - Key Quotes
b: Key Quotes Mrs Appleyard: She had come to ‘depend so much on Greta McCraw’ and her ‘masculine mind’. Mrs Appleyard: ‘How could she allow herself to be spirited away?’

t: Mrs Appleyard and Miss McCraw - Key Ideas
b: Key Ideas The limits of reason Dependence and control

Mademoiselle and Miss Lumley The two junior teachers are visual opposites: Mademoiselle wears lace, pearls and softly waving hair, while Miss Lumley wears plaid, spectacles and muddy colours. Mademoiselle goes to the picnic; Miss Lumley, like Sarah, is left behind. Mademoiselle has the courage to stand up to Mrs Appleyard and stays to the end; Miss Lumley is too afraid until she finally resigns.

t: Mademoiselle and Miss Lumley - Key Quotes
b: Key Quotes Miss Lumley: Irma’s discovery is ‘wonderful news’. Mademoiselle: Irma is ‘prettier than ever’.

t: Mademoiselle and Miss Lumley - Key Ideas
b: Key Ideas Appearance versus reality Fear of authority Curiosity and the need for answers

Irma and the Other Girls When Irma returns, the girls who once envied and admired her surround her in the gymnasium demanding ‘Tell us, Irma!’. Her vivid red dress sets her apart from their white uniforms. The scene turns into a frightening display of mob behaviour, showing how quickly civilised behaviour collapses when people are desperate for answers.

b: Key Ideas Mass hysteria and mob mentality The desire for certainty The collapse of civility
Scene Summaries and Analyses The sequences below follow the order of the film. Use them to locate evidence quickly; the Analysis notes suggest how each sequence connects to the big ideas.

Sequence 1 : The Opening Summary : Hanging Rock emerges from mist while Miranda’s voice-over says ‘What we see and what we seem are but a dream, a dream within a dream.’ A title card gives precise factual details about the disappearance. Appleyard College is then shown framed against a foreground of wild summer grass. Analysis : The order is significant. We see the Rock first, then the facts, then the college. From the outset Weir establishes the three forces of the film: nature as a fundamental force, the human need for factual order, and civilisation. The facts tell us what happened but not why, so the film begins with the mystery already unsolved.

Sequence 2 : St Valentine’s Morning Summary : The girls dress, lace each other’s corsets, and exchange Valentine cards and poems. Miranda and Sarah share a tender moment. Flowers are everywhere. Mrs Appleyard addresses the girls about gloves, snakes, ‘tomboy foolishness’ and returning ‘at about 8’. Sarah is told she is not to go on the picnic. Analysis : Weir portrays the students as elegant, refined and innocent, but also sheltered, uniform and restrained. The cultivated flowers represent a version of nature that has been domesticated and controlled. Mrs Appleyard’s warnings reveal an institutional fear of disorder, danger and lost time.

Sequence 3 : The Picnic Summary : The drag, driven by Mr Hussey, carries the girls, Miss McCraw and Mademoiselle to the Rock. Miranda opens a gate to let the party through. The picnic is laid out with cake, china and white dresses. Nearby, Colonel and Mrs Fitzhubert picnic with their nephew Michael and their groom Albert. Mr Hussey’s and Miss McCraw’s watches are found stopped at twelve. Much of the party grows drowsy and falls asleep. Analysis : The picnic and the characters’ clothing appear incongruous against the ancient landscape; civilised behaviour seems intrusive or strangely detached from the wilderness. The gate is the first threshold between the familiar world and the unknown. The stopped watches signal that the Rock operates outside measured, human time.

Sequence 4 : The Climb Summary : Miranda, Marion, Irma and Edith get permission to take measurements at the base of the Rock. Michael watches them cross the stream; Albert makes crude remarks. The girls climb higher, the rocks becoming increasingly maze-like. Near the top they fall asleep, then wake. Miranda, Marion and Irma, now without shoes and stockings, walk between two great rocks. Edith screams and runs back down. Miss McCraw is seen climbing alone. Analysis : Successive thresholds (the gate, the stream, the narrowing passages) create the sense that the Rock is drawing the girls towards it. Miranda’s line that ‘everything begins and ends at exactly the right time and place’ suggests acceptance of a different kind of time, while Edith’s ‘when are we going home?’ clings to ordinary chronology. Shedding clothes signals liberation from social convention.

t: Sequence 5 : The Return of the Drag
b: Sequence 5 : The Return of the Drag Summary : The drag arrives back at the college late at night. Mrs Appleyard, who has been waiting, hears from Mr Hussey that ‘nobody knows what happened... we were all asleep.’ Analysis : The schedule Mrs Appleyard imposed has collapsed. Mr Hussey’s admission that everyone was asleep suggests that the rational, conscious mind was absent at the very moment of the event, an early sign that reason will not provide an answer.

Sequence 6 : The Investigation Summary : Sergeant Bumpher leads the inquiry. Edith is examined by the doctor and asked ‘Was there a man?’ Mrs Bumpher reports that the town believes ‘it couldn’t be local.’ Michael first says he saw three girls, then four. Asked what he was thinking of as the girls crossed the creek, he points to a swan vase. Edith returns to the Rock and remembers a red cloud and Miss McCraw climbing in her drawers; Bumpher fixates on the missing skirt. Search parties, a tracker and dogs comb the Rock. Analysis : Each line of inquiry looks for an explanation that fits society’s assumptions: a male attacker, an outsider, a sexual crime. Memory proves unreliable. Bumpher’s dismissal of the red cloud shows that the authorities seek only the kind of explanation that fits their worldview. The film suggests rational thinking can be more concerned with preserving a sense of control than with discovering the truth.

Sequence 7 : Michael’s Search Summary : Against Albert’s advice, Michael rides to the Rock and searches alone, staying overnight. He becomes disoriented, struggles to climb and falls asleep. Albert finds him dazed and injured, clutching a scrap of lace. Following Michael’s trail, Albert discovers Irma alive. Analysis : Michael succeeds where the official searches failed, perhaps because he is guided by emotion and intuition rather than logic. Yet the Rock also overwhelms him, rewarding curiosity while frustrating the desire for certainty.

Sequence 8 : Irma Recovers Summary : Irma recuperates at the Fitzhuberts’ home, shrouded beneath white gauzy fabric. The doctor tells Bumpher her condition is ‘very strange.’ She cannot remember what happened. The townspeople gather, demanding ‘we’ve got a right to know.’ At the college, Miss Lumley calls the news ‘wonderful’; Mrs Appleyard says it ‘makes it worse.’ Analysis : Irma’s return should solve the mystery but instead deepens it. Her lost memory denies rational explanation even to someone who was there. Mrs Appleyard’s reaction reveals her real priority: one survivor with no story is worse for the college than a clear answer of any kind.

Sequence 9 : ‘Tell Us, Irma!’ Summary : Before leaving for Europe, Irma visits the college in a vivid red dress. In the gymnasium, where Sarah has been strapped to the wall to cure her stooping, the girls surround Irma demanding answers. The scene becomes hysterical; Miss Lumley cowers behind the piano and Mademoiselle intervenes, slapping Edith. Analysis : Irma’s red links her to the red cloud and suggests she has been transformed. The scene exposes the breakdown of social conventions: fear of the unknown and desperation for answers turn the ‘refined’ young ladies into a mob. Sarah’s literal restraint is a stark image of the college’s oppressive control.

Sequence 10 : The College Unravels Summary : Parents withdraw their daughters. Miss Lumley resigns. Mrs Appleyard drinks alone and tells Sarah she must return to the orphanage. Sarah is later found dead in the greenhouse by the head gardener. That night Albert dreams of his ‘kid sister’. Mrs Appleyard tells Mademoiselle that Sarah’s guardian collected her. Analysis : The greatest damage comes not from the Rock but from within the institution. Mrs Appleyard’s need for control turns into cruelty, and the most vulnerable person pays for it. Her lie about Sarah shows her preserving appearances to the end.

Sequence 11 : The Ending Summary : At dinner, Mrs Appleyard, dressed more softly than ever before, reminisces about Bournemouth, where ‘nothing changed – ever,’ and wonders how Miss McCraw could ‘allow herself to be spirited away.’ A final voice-over reports that the searches continued without result and that Mrs Appleyard died ‘while attempting to climb the rock.’ The film closes on slow-motion images of the picnic, with Miranda turning to wave. Analysis : Mrs Appleyard, the film’s champion of order, is finally drawn to the Rock herself. Her dishevelled hair and black mourning clothes contrast with her immaculate appearance at the start. The closing return to the picnic, filmed to resemble old footage, leaves the audience suspended in the moment before the disappearance, and suggests that nature is timeless while society can be disrupted and destroyed.
Film Techniques

List of Techniques Film Techniques in Picnic at Hanging Rock Technique Definition / Effect Example in the film Extreme long shot Shows a subject from a great distance, often dwarfed by its surroundings. The girls appear tiny against the towering pinnacles of the Rock, emphasising human insignificance. Low-angle shot Camera looks up at a subject, making it seem powerful or threatening. The Rock is frequently shot from below, so it towers over and dominates the characters. High-angle shot Camera looks down on a subject, making it seem small or vulnerable. Marion looks down on the picnickers ‘like a lot of ants’; Mrs Appleyard is often positioned above others. Framing How elements are arranged within the frame to direct attention or suggest relationships. Characters are enveloped by foliage or enclosed by rock walls, appearing subsumed by nature. Slow motion Footage played slower than real time, creating a dreamlike or significant effect. Miranda at the stream and the final picnic images, suggesting a moment outside ordinary time. Soft focus and diffused light Blurred edges and hazy light that soften the image. The morning at Appleyard and the picnic glow like paintings, idealising the girls and the bush. Dissolve One image fades gradually into another, linking them. Michael’s swan vase gives way to Miranda and then to a real swan, linking the three. Voice-over Narration heard over the images. Miranda’s opening ‘dream within a dream’; the closing report of Mrs Appleyard’s death

Framing the Rock How Weir frames the Rock is one of the most reusable pieces of evidence in the film. The camera presents the Rock as something that acts on the characters. Useful vocabulary: What the Rock does (verbs): towers over, dwarfs, encloses, conceals, swallows, lures, beckons, traps, dominates, overwhelms. What the Rock is (nouns): labyrinth, barrier, gateway, prison, predator, refuge, mystery, force, portal, wilderness. What the Rock is like (adjectives): towering, ancient, mysterious, claustrophobic, menacing, alluring, hypnotic, overwhelming, otherworldly, unknowable. How characters are framed within nature: vulnerable, subsumed, enveloped, immersed, diminished, overshadowed. ‘Through low-angle shots that make the Rock tower over the climbing girls, Weir portrays nature as an ancient, dominating force that dwarfs human ambition.’

Sound and Music The soundtrack is one of Weir’s main tools for creating mystery. Notice how each element connects to an idea: Classical music (such as Beethoven) – the human construct of measurable time and European order imposed on beauty. Pan pipes – the timelessness and haunting allure of nature; liberation from social convention. The string quartet and parlour music – the constraints of etiquette and the preservation of social hierarchy. The thrumming of the Rock – the inexplicable power of the natural world and its ancient rhythms. Shrieking, insistent noise – human horror and discomfort in the face of the unknowable. Ticking clocks – humanity’s desire to measure, schedule and control. ‘Through the soundtrack, Weir demonstrates that humanity’s obsession with measuring time is ultimately pointless when compared with the timelessness of nature.’

Those who climb remove hats, gloves, shoes and stockings; Edith keeps hers on. Mrs Appleyard: dark, severe dresses, an ornate, old-fashioned hairstyle and a watch pinned to her chest. Later she wears a brooch with her late husband’s photograph, and at the end her carefully arranged hair becomes dishevelled. Miss McCraw: a dark red dress and a veil to keep flies off her face. Mademoiselle: lace blouses, frills, pearls, lace gloves and softly waving hair – elegant and romantic. Miss Lumley: plaid, simple printed blouses, spectacles and muddy colours – sensible, muted, utilitarian. Irma’s return: a vivid red dress among the white uniforms, linking her to the red cloud and marking her transformation. Uniforms: the police, the doctor and the searchers (including the Indigenous tracker in a red coat) are identified by their roles, showing how society organises people by function and class.

Through his framing of the ancient Rock, his treatment of time and the haunting soundscape of the film, Weir presents a landscape that is at once enchanting and menacing to the members of colonial society who visit it. Ultimately, the film suggests that nature’s allure and its danger come from the same source: it lies beyond the reach of human understanding and control. Introduction and Context

Overview The Lottery and Other Stories (1949) is Shirley Jackson’s only collection of short stories published in her lifetime. Its twenty-five stories are mostly set in ordinary places: New York apartments, offices, buses and trains, small towns and suburban streets. Jackson finds something unsettling in each of them. Her characters are lonely, dissatisfied or anxious to fit in, and her communities are polite on the surface but capable of exclusion, prejudice and violence. The collection ends with its most famous story, ‘The Lottery’, in which a friendly village gathers on a sunny morning to stone one of its own.

t: America After the Second World War
b: America After the Second World War The stories were written in the 1940s, in the years during and immediately after the Second World War. Post-war America prized stability, prosperity and conformity: suburbs expanded, the ideal family was a breadwinning husband and a homemaking wife, and pressure to fit in was intense. At the same time, the war had revealed how ordinary people could take part in organised cruelty, and the late 1940s saw growing suspicion of anyone considered different or disloyal.

t: America After the Second World War - Analysis
b: Analysis Jackson’s stories expose the anxieties beneath this ideal of order. Her communities enforce sameness, punish difference and turn on outsiders. When you write about conformity, social judgement or ‘the violence beneath a civilised society’, you are writing about fears that were very much alive when Jackson wrote.

Gender Roles Middle-class women in the 1940s were expected to marry, keep house and raise children; single women in the city, like the protagonists of ‘The Daemon Lover’ and ‘The Villager’, lived with the anxiety of ageing outside these expectations. Men were expected to be confident, practical and dominant.

Analysis Many of Jackson’s characters struggle with these roles. Some, like David in ‘Like Mother Used to Make’ or the restless women of ‘The Tooth’ and ‘Elizabeth’, do not fit them; others, like Tessie Hutchinson with her dishes in the sink, play them dutifully until it is too late. Jackson shows both the pressure to conform and the price of conforming.

Race and Prejudice America in the 1940s was deeply segregated, and racism was often expressed through polite, respectable behaviour rather than open hostility. Two stories, ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’ and ‘Flower Garden’, examine this directly.

Analysis Jackson is interested in the gap between how people see themselves and how they behave. Mrs Wilson thinks she is generous; the people of the town think they are protecting their community. Both stories show prejudice maintained by people who believe themselves to be good.

The Reception of ‘The Lottery’ ‘The Lottery’ was first published in The New Yorker in June 1948. It provoked one of the largest reader responses in the magazine’s history: hundreds of letters, many angry, confused or disturbed, and some asking where such lotteries were held. Readers were shocked that a story could show ordinary, likeable people carrying out a murder as calmly as a town meeting.
Analysis The reaction proves Jackson’s point. Readers recognised the village as their own, which is exactly what made the story so disturbing. Its power comes from its ordinariness.

t: Shirley Jackson and the Short Story
b: Shirley Jackson and the Short Story

Shirley Jackson (1916–1965) Shirley Jackson was born in San Francisco and spent most of her adult life in North Bennington, Vermont, where her husband, the critic Stanley Edgar Hyman, taught at Bennington College. She raised four children while writing novels, short stories and humorous accounts of family life. As an outsider in a small New England town, she experienced the kind of suspicion and gossip her stories depict. She is best known today for ‘The Lottery’ and for her novels The Haunting of Hill House (1959) and We Have Always Lived in the Castle (1962), and is regarded as a major writer of psychological suspense and the uncanny.

Why the Short Story? A short story has little room for explanation. Jackson uses this to her advantage. She often: opens with a description of the protagonist’s ordinary routine or a pleasant setting; introduces an unexpected event, stranger or disruption; lets tension build through small, everyday details and dialogue; ends abruptly, often with the protagonist excluded, defeated or trapped, and without explaining what it all means. The reader is left to fill the silence, and that is where much of the unease comes from.

t: Reading the Collection as a Whole
b: Reading the Collection as a Whole Although each story stands alone, the collection is designed to be read together. A figure named James Harris (or Jim, or Jamie) appears in many stories in different guises: a missing fiancé, a writer, a dinner guest, a neighbour, a stranger in a blue suit. The book is divided into parts introduced by epigraphs from Joseph Glanvill’s seventeenth-century treatise on witchcraft, and ends with an epilogue: verses from the old ballad ‘James Harris, The Daemon Lover’, in which a mysterious lover carries a woman away to her doom.

t: Reading the Collection as a Whole - Analysis
b: Analysis These links suggest that the strangeness in each story is part of a larger pattern. James Harris works almost like a demon or tempter who drifts through ordinary lives, exposing the dissatisfaction and fear already present beneath the surface. In essays, connecting stories through these recurring figures and motifs shows the examiners that you understand the collection, not just individual stories.

t: How the Stories Can Be Grouped
b: How the Stories Can Be Grouped This guide concentrates on twelve stories that together cover the collection’s key ideas. A useful way to study them is in groups: Discontent and identity: ‘The Daemon Lover’, ‘Like Mother Used to Make’, ‘The Villager’ Cruelty taught and normalised: ‘The Witch’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘Charles’ Insiders and outsiders: ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’, ‘Flower Garden’ Challenging or yielding to expectations: ‘Elizabeth’, ‘The Tooth’, ‘Of Course’ The anchor story: ‘The Lottery’

Unexpected Events Expose Our Struggles Jackson uses unexpected events and strangers to expose characters’ hidden fears, insecurities and dissatisfaction with their lives. A fiancé fails to arrive; a stranger knocks on the door; a man on a train tells a child a violent story. The disruption does not create the problem so much as reveal what was already there.

Insecurity and Dissatisfaction Jackson shows how people feel uncertain about their identities and dissatisfied with their lives, often imagining that another life might make them happier. The protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ is ‘not satisfied with her clothes, her face, her apartment’; Miss Clarence in ‘The Villager’ once wanted to be a dancer; Clara Spencer in ‘The Tooth’ drifts away from her own identity altogether.

Social Judgement and Exclusion Jackson explores how social expectations pressure people to conform and leave those who do not fit in feeling judged, anxious and excluded. Mrs MacLane is frozen out of the town in ‘Flower Garden’; Mrs Walpole fears her neighbours in ‘The Renegade’; Tessie Hutchinson is cast out in the most final way possible.

t: The Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society
b: The Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society Jackson reveals how violence, cruelty and hostility can exist beneath the polite and orderly surface of everyday life. Physical violence features in only a few stories, so think of this idea more broadly: cruelty, insensitivity, aggressive intolerance and a lack of compassion. Strangers mock, neighbours gossip, children learn to relish violence, and a whole village picks up stones.

Endings Jackson’s stories often end grimly, and these endings are some of the most useful evidence you have. Compare: ‘The Daemon Lover’: ‘No matter how often or how firmly she knocked, no one ever came to the door.’ ‘Like Mother Used to Make’: David thinks miserably of his own warm home and hears faintly down the hall the sound of laughter. ‘The Villager’: ‘Her shoulders ached.’ ‘The Witch’: ‘Probably he was a witch.’ ‘The Renegade’: Mrs Walpole closes her eyes, ‘suddenly feeling the harsh hands pulling her down, the sharp points closing in on her throat.’ ‘Flower Garden’: Mrs Winning ‘swung around without speaking and started, with great dignity, back up the hill toward the old Winning house.’ ‘The Lottery’: ‘It isn’t fair, it isn’t right,’ Mrs. Hutchinson screamed, and then they were upon her. Some endings shut characters out (exclusion); some leave them trapped in disappointment (defeat and resignation); some show cruelty becoming normal. Very few offer justice or resolution.
Language and Style

An Understated, Ordinary Voice Jackson writes in a plain, calm, almost conversational style. She describes terrible things in the same tone as a morning’s errands. In ‘The Lottery’, the stoning is introduced through the same matter-of-fact narration as the gathering of the villagers and their chat about tractors and taxes. This flatness is deliberate: by refusing to signal horror, Jackson makes the reader feel the horror of how normal cruelty has become.

Everyday Detail Jackson builds her worlds from small, concrete details: coffee, dishes in the sink, the neat chairs in David’s apartment, a lollipop, a bus ticket. These details make the settings feel real and familiar, which is what makes the disruptions so unsettling. They also carry meaning: the protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ repeatedly finds ‘nothing to eat’, and her lack of appetite suggests the emptiness of her life.

Dialogue and Polite Speech Characters in Jackson’s stories are often unfailingly polite while saying cruel or prejudiced things. Mrs Wilson’s generosity in ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’ is full of assumptions; the neighbours in ‘The Renegade’ cheerfully suggest ways to kill a dog; Mrs Harris in ‘Of Course’ imposes her views through ‘seemingly friendly conversation’. Listen for the gap between the tone of what is said and what it means.

Irony Irony runs through the collection: a lottery whose ‘prize’ is death; a sunny summer day for a murder; a title, ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’, that mocks performative politeness; a mother in ‘Charles’ who never suspects the badly behaved boy is her own son.

Unnamed and Symbolic Names Some characters have no name at all: the protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’, ‘the little boy’ in ‘The Witch’. This makes them seem anonymous and interchangeable, as if their stories could belong to anyone. Other names are pointed: Laurie suggests a crown of laurels, a symbol of glory; Walpole has been read as meaning ‘foreigner’; Clara means ‘clear’ or ‘bright’; Mrs Winning belongs to the family that always wins.

Setting and Weather Jackson often sets disturbing events against pleasant weather. The village of ‘The Lottery’ gathers on a ‘clear and sunny’ morning ‘with the fresh warmth of a full-summer day’. Ask whether the weather in a story reinforces ordinary life, contrasts with it, mirrors the characters’ feelings, or creates an ironic contrast with them.

Open Endings Jackson rarely explains. We never learn what happened to Jamie Harris, who the man on the train really was, or where Clara Spencer is going. The reader is left uneasy, and must decide for themselves what the story reveals.
Story Summaries and Analyses The collection contains twenty-five stories. The twelve below are the key stories for essays: learn them well enough to use them flexibly across many topics.

‘The Daemon Lover’ Summary : On the morning she is to marry Jamie Harris, an unnamed woman of thirty-four prepares anxiously, changing her dress, tidying her apartment and stocking food for their new life. Jamie does not arrive. She goes looking for him, questioning shopkeepers, a newspaper seller and neighbours, who respond with indifference, suspicion or mockery. Following vague leads, she reaches an apartment building where she thinks she hears voices and laughter behind a door, but no one answers her knocking. Analysis : The protagonist is defined by deep-seated dissatisfaction: she is ‘not satisfied with her clothes, her face, her apartment’ and hopes marriage will transform her life. The recurring lack of food (‘There was nothing to eat in the apartment’) suggests a life that is empty and hollow. ‘Daemon’ can mean demon, but also a guiding or inspiring spirit; Jamie is both, offering hope and then vanishing cruelly. The casual cruelty of strangers (‘the boy grinned insolently at her’) shows how easily individual suffering is dismissed. The ending, with the door that never opens, is one of Jackson’s starkest images of exclusion.

‘Like Mother Used to Make’ Summary : David Turner keeps a neat, carefully chosen apartment and enjoys cooking and domestic order. His neighbour Marcia is loud, untidy and always hungry. David invites her to dinner and bakes a pie. When Mr Harris, a man from Marcia’s office, knocks, Marcia lets him assume the apartment and the cooking are hers. David, unable to assert himself, is gradually pushed out and ends up retreating to Marcia’s cluttered apartment, hearing laughter from his own home down the hall. Analysis : Jackson contrasts David’s control (‘small, quick movements’, ‘the neat small table and four careful chairs’) with Marcia’s disorder (‘Marcia arrived with a shout and fresh air and disorder’). David’s pleasure in domestic activities challenges traditional ideas of masculinity, and his passivity leaves him excluded from his own home. The title is ironic: the comforts of home ‘like mother used to make’ are made by a man and claimed by a woman who did not make them.

‘The Villager’ Summary : Miss Hilda Clarence, a woman in her thirties who came to New York hoping to be a dancer, now works in an office. She visits an apartment to look at furniture for sale. While waiting, she is mistaken for the owner by a visitor named Harris, and slips into the role, inventing a life as a ‘dancer’. After he leaves, she returns to her own reality. Analysis : Harris’s unexpected arrival is the catalyst that exposes Miss Clarence’s disappointment with her life. She tells herself she has ‘a good job’ and lives ‘better than she would in her home town’, but her compulsive lie reveals her desire to be seen as someone more accomplished and interesting. The final line, ‘Her shoulders ached’, suggests the weight of carrying unfulfilled dreams.

‘The Witch’ Summary : A little boy travels by train with his mother and baby sister, looking out the window. A friendly stranger sits beside him and, encouraged by the boy’s questions, tells a gruesome story about killing his own little sister. The mother is horrified, but the boy is delighted. When the man leaves, the mother tries to explain it away, and the boy decides ‘Probably he was a witch.’ Analysis : The story shows how children learn what behaviour is normal. The baby ‘strapped securely to the seat’ and the boy rewarded with a lollipop suggest a world of control and reward, yet the boy greets violence with breathless excitement (‘Did you cut her all in pieces?’). The cruelty arrives in a pleasant, everyday setting, which makes it more disturbing. The boy’s final explanation turns real violence into a fairy tale.

‘The Renegade’ Summary : Mrs Walpole, new to the country, learns that her family’s dog, Lady, has been killing a neighbour’s chickens. As she goes about the town, neighbours offer increasingly cruel advice for curing or punishing the dog, including tying a dead chicken around her neck or fitting her with a spiked collar. When her own children eagerly describe how the spikes would cut the dog’s head off, Mrs Walpole feels as though she is being attacked herself. Analysis : A renegade is someone who rejects conventional behaviour; the dog is one, but so in a sense is Mrs Walpole, an outsider in the community. The neighbours’ casual enthusiasm normalises violence, and her children’s delight shows how readily cruelty is passed on. The ending, ‘the harsh hands pulling her down, the sharp points closing in on her throat’, transfers the punishment from the dog to the woman, revealing her fear of the community’s judgement.

‘Charles’ Summary : Laurie starts kindergarten and comes home each day with stories about a boy called Charles who misbehaves dreadfully. His parents are fascinated and amused, and ‘Charles’ becomes a family byword. At the parent-teacher meeting, Laurie’s mother looks for Charles’s mother, only to learn from the teacher that there is no Charles in the class. Analysis : Laurie invents an identity to conceal his own bad behaviour, and his mother’s unquestioning acceptance shows how parents see what they want to see. The twist exposes the gap between appearance and reality, and the comic tone hides a sharper point about how adults misread, and help create, children’s behaviour.

‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’ Summary : Johnny brings his friend Boyd, a Black boy, home for lunch. Johnny’s mother, Mrs Wilson, assumes Boyd’s family is poor, his father a labourer, and his mother overworked, and offers him charity he does not need. Boyd politely corrects each assumption. Mrs Wilson becomes offended when he declines her old clothes, while the boys, untroubled, carry on with their game. Analysis : The title comes from a comic strip about two absurdly polite Frenchmen who keep deferring to each other; the boys use it to play at manners. Jackson uses it ironically to expose the gap between outward politeness and genuine respect. Mrs Wilson believes she is being kind, but her ‘kindness’ is built on racist stereotypes, and her defensiveness shows how entrenched they are.

‘Flower Garden’ Summary : Young Mrs Winning, who has married into the town’s oldest family and lives under her mother-in-law’s control in the old Winning house, befriends Mrs MacLane, a widow who moves into the cottage she herself once dreamed of owning. The two women grow close, and their sons play together. When Mrs MacLane hires a Black man, Mr Jones, to help with her garden, the town turns against her, and Mrs Winning, fearing association, abandons her. Analysis : The townspeople act as gatekeepers, advising Mrs Winning to speak to Mrs MacLane ‘about that colored man’. Mrs MacLane recognises what is happening: ‘Pretty soon they... they’ll tell someone else to speak to me.’ Children reveal the town’s values: Howard’s racist name-calling towards Billy Jones shows how early prejudice is learned. The ending, as Mrs Winning walks ‘with great dignity’ back to the old house, shows conformity winning over friendship.

‘Elizabeth’ Summary : Elizabeth Style works for a struggling literary agency in New York, in a relationship with her business partner that has lost its warmth, and in a life far from the success she once imagined. When a new secretary arrives, Elizabeth feels her position slipping. The story ends with her making a dinner date with Jim Harris, who she hopes might help launch a new career. Analysis : Elizabeth’s story is one of insecurity and quiet despair beneath a professional surface. Her plans with Harris represent the possibility of another life, but the reader suspects they are another illusion. Like the protagonists of ‘The Daemon Lover’ and ‘The Villager’, she pins her hopes on a man who may never deliver.

‘The Tooth’ Summary : Clara Spencer takes an overnight bus to New York to see a dentist about a painful tooth. Dazed by codeine and lack of sleep, she meets a man in a blue suit, Jim, who speaks of a beautiful faraway place. In the city, her sense of self dissolves; she cannot remember details of her own life and must find her name written on her belongings. At the end she runs barefoot through hot sand, hand in hand with Jim. Analysis : Jim represents Clara’s desire to escape her ordinary, grey life. His poetic visions (‘the waves ringing on the shores like bells’, ‘the grass is so green and so soft’) evoke a mythical place far from bus stations and dentists’ rooms. Clara’s name means ‘clear’ or ‘bright’, ironic for a woman whose identity has faded. Unusually, the ending suggests escape from social expectations rather than defeat, though whether it is liberation or madness is left open.

‘Of Course’ Summary : Mrs Tylor watches new neighbours move in next door and decides from their furniture and clothes that they are ‘nice people, obviously’. When she speaks to Mrs Harris, however, she learns that the family does not allow movies, radio or newspapers. Mrs Tylor, unsettled, finds herself agreeing politely. Analysis : The story turns on the pressure of neighbourliness. Mrs Tylor’s first judgements are based on appearances; Mrs Harris then projects her own rigid views through friendly conversation (‘it means such a lot to have really thoughtful neighbours’). Social conformity and the appearance of politeness are maintained, despite the intolerance beneath them.

‘The Lottery’ Summary : On the morning of June 27th, the villagers of a small farming community gather in the square for their annual lottery. Children collect stones. Mr Summers runs the drawing from a battered black box. Tessie Hutchinson arrives late, joking that she forgot what day it was. Heads of families draw slips of paper; Bill Hutchinson draws the marked slip. Tessie protests that it ‘wasn’t fair’, and in a second drawing among the Hutchinson family she draws the paper with the black spot. The villagers, including her friends and children, stone her. Analysis : ‘The Lottery’ is the anchor story of the collection: it shows every key idea. The pleasant setting (‘clear and sunny’) makes the violence more shocking. The ritual is maintained by authority figures (Mr Summers, Mr Graves), defended by Old Man Warner (‘There’s always been a lottery’), and carried out by ordinary people. Mr Adams mentions villages that have given up the lottery, yet still joins in. Tessie is no rebel: she accepts the lottery until it threatens her. The detail that ‘although the villagers had forgotten the ritual and lost the original black box, they still remembered to use stones’ suggests that the violence outlives any meaning the tradition once had.

b: The Violence Beneath a Civilised Society ‘The Lottery’: ‘The morning of June 27th was clear and sunny, with the fresh warmth of a full-summer day.’ ‘The Lottery’: ‘Bobby Martin had already stuffed his pockets full of stones.’ ‘The Lottery’: Mrs Hutchinson: ‘Clean forgot what day it was.’ ‘The Lottery’: Mrs Hutchinson: ‘Wouldn’t have me leave m’dishes in the sink, now, would you, Joe?’ ‘The Lottery’: Mrs Hutchinson: ‘Get up there, Bill.’ ‘The Lottery’: Old Man Warner: ‘Lottery in June, corn be heavy soon.’ ‘The Lottery’: Old Man Warner: ‘There’s always been a lottery.’ ‘The Lottery’: Mrs Hutchinson: ‘You didn’t give him time enough to take any paper he wanted. I saw you. It wasn’t fair!’ ‘The Lottery’: Bill Hutchinson: ‘Shut up, Tessie.’ ‘The Lottery’: Mrs Hutchinson: ‘I think we ought to start over.’ ‘The Lottery’: ‘Although the villagers had forgotten the ritual and lost the original black box, they still remembered to use stones.’ ‘The Lottery’: ‘Mrs. Delacroix selected a stone so large she had to pick it up with both hands.’ ‘The Lottery’: ‘Come on,’ she said. ‘Hurry up.’ ‘The Lottery’: ‘Come on, come on, everyone.’ ‘The Lottery’: ‘It isn’t fair, it isn’t right,’ Mrs. Hutchinson screamed, and then they were upon her. ‘The Renegade’: ‘The spikes cut her head off.’ ‘The Renegade’: ‘They both began to laugh...’ ‘The Renegade’: ‘Mrs. Walpole closed her eyes, suddenly feeling the harsh hands pulling her down, the sharp points closing in on her throat.’
Theme Analysis

Insecurity and Dissatisfaction Jackson’s protagonists are frequently discontented. The woman in ‘The Daemon Lover’ suffers from deep-seated dissatisfaction, anxiety about her appearance and ageing, and insecurity about her desirability; she hopes marriage will let her reinvent herself. Miss Clarence in ‘The Villager’ disguises her disappointment that she never became a dancer. Elizabeth Style pins her hopes on Jim Harris. Clara Spencer escapes her grey life entirely, at the cost of her identity. Jackson suggests that these characters’ unhappiness is shaped both by society and by themselves. Social expectations about marriage, success and femininity set the standards they fail to meet, but their own fantasies of another life deepen their dissatisfaction. As one useful interpretation puts it, the protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ intensifies her own unhappiness through her thoughts, choices and actions, while the happiness of others accentuates her dissatisfaction.

Social Judgement and Exclusion Jackson’s communities decide who belongs. People who challenge social expectations are judged, excluded or punished: Mrs MacLane for employing Mr Jones, Mrs Walpole for her uncontrolled dog, David for failing to be the right kind of man. Insiders police the boundaries out of fear of becoming outsiders themselves: Mrs Winning abandons her friend because she is anxious about losing belonging and respectability. Useful vocabulary: conformity, gatekeepers, ostracise, marginalise, alienated, exclusionary, respectability, social status .

Unexpected Events Expose Our Struggles A stranger arrives, a fiancé disappears, a dog kills chickens, a man on a train tells a story. In each case, the disruption exposes problems that already existed beneath the surface: Miss Clarence’s disappointment, David’s passivity, Mrs Walpole’s fear of her neighbours, the mother’s inability to control what her son learns. James Harris, who appears in story after story, embodies this idea: he enters characters’ lives unexpectedly and reveals the gap between how they see themselves and how others see them. Useful vocabulary: catalyst, disruption, destabilise, unravel, expose, vulnerability .

t: The Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society
b: The Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society Physical violence features in only a few stories (‘The Witch’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘The Lottery’), so think of this idea as including cruelty, insensitivity, intolerance and lack of compassion. Jackson’s violence is often: Arbitrary – based on chance rather than any fair reason, like the lottery’s random selection; Ritualised – performed according to tradition, like the annual drawing; Normalised – treated as ordinary even when it is harmful, like the neighbours’ advice in ‘The Renegade’; Entrenched – so established that it is difficult to change, like the racism of ‘Flower Garden’. Jackson repeatedly shows that the most disturbing cruelty comes from ordinary, respectable people: friendly neighbours, polite mothers, children. Children both reveal the hidden prejudices of adults and occasionally resist them, highlighting the flaws in adult values.

Conformity and Tradition Many stories show a chain of social pressure: society establishes rules about how people should behave; adults teach children what is normal; fear of punishment pressures people to conform; people come to accept the rules without questioning them; and harmful attitudes are passed from one generation to the next. In ‘The Lottery’, even little Davy Hutchinson is given pebbles.
Character Analysis

The Protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ Unnamed and thirty-four, she is anxious, self-critical and desperate to be transformed by marriage. Her search for Jamie exposes her to the indifference and mockery of strangers. She represents the collection’s lonely women, shut out from the happiness they long for.

t: David Turner and Marcia (‘Like Mother Used to Make’)
b: David Turner and Marcia (‘Like Mother Used to Make’) David is careful, controlled and highly organised, finding pleasure in domestic order traditionally coded as feminine. Marcia is careless, loud and hungry, comfortable taking what is not hers. Their contrast challenges gender expectations, and David’s inability to assert himself leaves him excluded from his own home.

Miss Clarence (‘The Villager’) A woman who came to the city with dreams and settled for a job. Her readiness to assume another person’s identity, and to call herself a dancer, reveals her longing to be seen as someone more interesting than she believes she is.

t: The Little Boy and the Stranger (‘The Witch’)
b: The Little Boy and the Stranger (‘The Witch’) The boy, never named, is fascinated rather than frightened by violence. The stranger, friendly and well-dressed, is a figure of casual menace. The mother tries and fails to protect her son from what he has heard.

Mrs Walpole (‘The Renegade’) An outsider in a country town, anxious to be accepted. As the community’s advice grows more violent, she comes to identify with the dog, and the story ends with her imagining the punishment closing in on her.

Laurie and His Mother (‘Charles’) Laurie projects his own misbehaviour onto an invented boy; his mother believes every word. Together they show how people misinterpret what is in front of them and see what they want to see.

t: Mrs Wilson (‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’)
b: Mrs Wilson (‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’) A well-meaning mother whose generosity rests on racial stereotypes. When Boyd challenges her assumptions, her defensiveness exposes how deeply entrenched her prejudice is.

t: Mrs Winning and Mrs MacLane (‘Flower Garden’)
b: Mrs Winning and Mrs MacLane (‘Flower Garden’) Mrs Winning longs for independence from her husband’s family but ultimately chooses conformity, abandoning her friend. Mrs MacLane, the outsider, behaves decently and is punished for it.

Elizabeth Style (‘Elizabeth’) A woman clinging to a failing career and a cooling relationship, anxious about being replaced. Her hopes in Jim Harris suggest that, like other Jackson protagonists, she imagines escape through someone else.

Clara Spencer (‘The Tooth’) A wife and mother whose identity dissolves on her journey to the dentist. Her escape with the man in the blue suit is one of the few endings in the collection that breaks free of social expectations, though it may also be a breakdown.
Mrs Tylor (‘Of Course’) Mrs Tylor judges her new neighbours by appearances, then feels pressured to agree with Mrs Harris’s rigid views. She shows how politeness can become a form of conformity.

Tessie Hutchinson (‘The Lottery’) Is Tessie a transgressor, victim or follower? She arrives late and jokes about the lottery, encourages her husband to ‘get up there’, and does not question the ritual until her family is chosen. She then protests that it ‘wasn’t fair’ and even tries to include her married daughter to improve her odds. She is chosen by chance, not for any crime, and is killed by friends and family. Most readers see her as a follower who becomes a victim: her protest is against her own selection, not against the lottery itself.

The Enforcers of ‘The Lottery’ Authority figures: Mr Summers and Mr Graves organise the lottery and keep it running efficiently. Defender of tradition: Old Man Warner criticises villages that want to give it up and insists ‘There’s always been a lottery.’ Social conformists: Mr Adams mentions villages that have stopped the lottery but still takes part in the stoning. Complicit participants: Mrs Delacroix, Tessie’s friend, chooses a stone so large she needs both hands; Bill Hutchinson silences his wife; the children gather stones.

James Harris Harris appears throughout the collection: as Jamie, the fiancé who vanishes in ‘The Daemon Lover’; as the visitor who prompts Miss Clarence’s lie in ‘The Villager’; as Marcia’s colleague in ‘Like Mother Used to Make’; as the man in the blue suit in ‘The Tooth’ (and a blue-suited stranger in ‘The Witch’); as the Harris family whose chickens die in ‘The Renegade’; as the neighbours in ‘Of Course’; and as Elizabeth’s dinner date. He enters characters’ lives unexpectedly, disrupts their routines and exposes problems that already exist. Some readers see him as a demon or tempter, the ‘daemon lover’ of the ballad that closes the book.

Introduction Shirley Jackson’s The Lottery and Other Stories (1949) is set in the most familiar places imaginable: city apartments, trains, small-town streets and village squares. Introduction From the very beginning of your schooling career, you have been introduced to several different methods of writing essays. Although all structures have their advantages and disadvantages, it is essential that you have a fool-proof method of writing essays for your end of year examination. Having a solid method of writing analytical essays and practicing these throughout the year will result in a strong foundation, enabling you to tackle any essay question with confidence. The key to success lies not only in understanding the content but also in being able to present your ideas in a clear, structured, and coherent manner. With a well-practised approach, you will be able to break down complex texts, analyse them effectively, and construct a well-supported argument that demonstrates both depth and clarity of thought. In the following, we will explore a structured approach to writing an analytical text response. By familiarising yourself with this framework, you will be better equipped to organise your ideas, manage your time efficiently, and ultimately maximise your performance in the exam.

t: What is Needed in an Essay
b: What is Needed in an Essay An essay is a structured piece of writing that presents an argument, analysis, or narrative on a particular topic. The purpose of an essay is to communicate a clear, well-reasoned point of view, often backed by evidence and examples. Essays are typically composed of several key parts: an introduction, body paragraphs, and a conclusion. Each section plays a specific role in conveying the writer’s ideas and helping the reader understand and engage with the topic at hand.

Introduction The introduction serves as the starting point of the essay, setting the stage for the discussion to follow. It introduces the topic, provides necessary background information, and presents the thesis statement, which outlines the main argument or purpose of the essay. A strong introduction grabs the reader’s attention, often through a compelling hook, and establishes the importance of the topic. It should also provide a clear roadmap of what the essay will cover, guiding the reader’s expectations and providing a sense of structure.

Body Paragraphs The body of an essay is where the main arguments or points are developed and supported with evidence, examples, or analysis. Typically, an essay contains three body paragraphs, although this can vary depending on the length and depth of the topic. Each paragraph should focus on a single aspect of the thesis statement and contribute to the overall argument.

Conclusion The conclusion is the final part of the essay, where the writer sums up the key points made in the body paragraphs and reinforces the thesis statement. It provides closure to the discussion and leaves a lasting impression on the reader. A strong conclusion restates the main argument in a fresh way, summarising the key insights presented in the essay. It may also offer suggestions for further exploration or suggest the broader implications of the topic.
Planning

Deconstructing the Prompt When first planning your essay, you must directly respond to the prompt that is presented to you, and consider the key authorial messages that could help you respond with insight. This involves three important steps: Find the key concepts. This will most likely correlate with the key concepts you have studied throughout the unit, you should also make sure to identify synonyms of these concepts too! Find any instructional verbs. These are words that instruct you to answer the prompt in a certain manner, in English the main verbs to look out for is discuss, do you agree, to what extent or how. Identify any expectations/limitations. These ore words that limit what you con include in your essays and set on expectation on what you should be discussing. Example prompt: ‘The dream sequences in Rainbow’s End are the characters’ only escape from the depressing reality of life.’ Do you agree? This is a very straightforward prompt—you need to demonstrate a multiple-sided response to what Harrison perceives as the role of dreams and aspirations in her characters’ lives. There are no limits to what should be discussed here, but you are expected to focus your discussion on the ideas of dreams, escape, and reality as they relate to the values, identities, and choices of Nan Dear, Gladys, and Dolly. Consider the historical context of 1950s assimilationist Australia, racism, class, and the characters’ evolving sense of agency throughout the play.

Contention Now that you understand what the prompt is asking, we can begin to think about what our interpretation of Harrison’s message is. Let’s consider the first prompt again: ‘The dream sequences in Rainbow’s End are the characters’ only escape from the depressing reality of life.’ Do you agree? We can approach this in multiple ways. Here are three simplistic interpretations (agree, disagree, somewhere in between): Harrison suggests that dreams offer the characters comfort, but they cannot change the reality of their circumstances. Harrison implies that dreams are the characters’ only refuge from a society that denies them dignity and opportunity. Harrison demonstrates that it is action, not dreaming, that ultimately allows the characters to escape their circumstances. However, these interpretations are quite general and lack specificity. They don’t tell the reader exactly what you are arguing. Let’s improve them with more precise language and deeper knowledge of the text: Harrison portrays dreams as both sustaining and limiting, suggesting that Gladys’s fantasies of meeting the Queen preserve her dignity while simultaneously revealing how deeply colonial ideals of acceptance have been internalised. Harrison implies that, for a family denied housing, education, and respect, the imagination becomes a vital site of survival and self-worth in a society that offers no material escape. It also directly links to the contention: that dreams sustain the characters, even in circumstances that offer no material escape.
